rationale: The CRC signal in Baxter mostly comes from a few oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is rare, so random-forest splits seldom pick it up. This change adds two pooled features, the log of their combined relative abundance and how many of them are present, so the forest gets one dense, strong feature that matches across studies by taxonomy name.

Most of the few hundred genera are present in only a handful of samples. Because the forest tries a random subset of about sqrt(p) features at each split, these near-empty columns waste many splits and add noise. This change keeps only genera detected (relative abundance > 1e-4) in at least 10% of the training fold, plus the pooled oral-marker features. The filter is decided inside each fold, so it uses no test data, and it works on taxonomy names, so it transfers to other studies.

Add one log-ratio feature: the pooled oral-pathogen abundance divided by the pooled abundance of butyrate-producing commensals (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Butyricicoccus, Coprococcus, Anaerostipes, ...). CRC stool tends to gain oral pathogens and lose these butyrate producers, so a single balance can capture both shifts in one feature that is independent of sequencing depth and composition and matches across studies by taxonomy name. The current pooled features only capture the gain side.

CRC stool usually has lower and less even diversity because commensals are lost. The model only sees this through rare genus columns, so I'm adding depth-robust alpha-diversity features: expected OTU richness at a fixed rarefaction depth (computed exactly, no random subsampling), plus OTU-level and genus-level Shannon entropy. These are dense, study-agnostic features the forest can split on directly.

Right now every OTU with no genus name (`g__`) is pooled into a single "g__" column, whatever family it belongs to. That mixes together large, biologically distinct groups such as unclassified Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae and Enterobacteriaceae. Unclassified Lachnospiraceae is one of the strongest CRC-depleted features in Baxter's own model. This change gives each unnamed genus a key from its deepest named rank (e.g. `f__Lachnospiraceae_unclassified`), so that signal stays separate and still matches across studies by taxonomy name.

The random forest only picks up a few strong splits (oral pathogens, diversity). The CRC-vs-healthy shift in many commensal genera is weak but adds up, and that kind of signal fits a linear model on log-ratio data better. This change adds an L2 logistic regression on CLR-transformed filtered genera plus the standardized engineered features. Its regularization is tuned by inner grouped CV on the training fold only, and its predictions are rank-averaged with the RF's so the two complementary models are blended.

Add a second compositional block to the logistic regression: CLR-transformed family-level abundances, prevalence-filtered inside each training fold. The genus CLR stays as it is. At family level, the many sparse or unclassified genera that share a shift (Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae lost; Fusobacteriaceae, Porphyromonadaceae and Peptostreptococcaceae gained in CRC) are pooled into denser, less noisy log-ratio features. Family names also match more reliably across studies than genus names do. Family features go only into the linear model, because splitting unclassified groups apart for the random forest hurt in round 5.

The CLR in the logistic regression currently fills every zero with the same pseudocount (1e-5), no matter how deeply the sample was sequenced. A zero in a 3k-read sample is "below about 3e-4", while a zero in a 50k-read sample is "below about 2e-5". With a fixed pseudocount, part of the log-ratio signal ends up tracking library size rather than biology. This change uses depth-aware multiplicative zero replacement: each zero becomes half a read, 0.5/N for that sample. Observed abundances are left unchanged. Library size is used only for this and is never a model feature.

CRC stool is often described as "dysbiotic": it drifts away from the healthy community in many inconsistent directions (the Anna Karenina idea). A linear model on CLR genera cannot express "far from healthy in any direction", and the forest only sees one feature at a time. This change adds a beta-diversity "dysbiosis index": the log of the Aitchison distance, with each genus scaled by the healthy spread, to the centroid of the healthy training samples. Training rows get it out-of-fold through grouped inner CV, so their own labels don't leak into it. The index is fed to both the forest and the logistic regression.

The L2 logistic regression currently shrinks every standardized feature by the same amount. That treats the oral-pathogen markers (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella and their pooled features), which have replicated across many CRC cohorts, the same as about 100 noisy commensal genera. This change applies an informative prior: it multiplies the marker columns by a factor so they are penalized less. The factor is chosen from {1, 2, 3, 5}, jointly with C, by inner grouped CV on the training fold only.

Add a third rank-averaged model: an L2 logistic regression on genus detection features. Each feature is the exact rarefied probability that the genus would be seen if the sample were subsampled to 1000 reads. In Baxter, much of the CRC signal (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas and many lost commensals) is whether a genus is there at all, not how much of it there is. These probabilities measure presence on the same footing for every sample, whatever its sequencing depth. The CLR model can't see this cleanly because of imputed zeros, and the forest can't because it splits on raw abundance.

The forest currently grows every tree to purity on about 230 samples with noisy compositional features, which gives jagged, overfit probability scores. For AUROC the ranking matters most, and smoother scores usually rank better. This change picks the forest's leaf size and per-split feature fraction by out-of-bag AUROC on the training fold only, so it needs no extra CV loops and never touches test labels.

The RF and the CLR logistic regression are currently blended 50/50 by rank. Their relative strength probably varies between training folds and between cohorts. This change picks the blend weight (limited to 0.3–0.7 so it can't drift far from equal and overfit) on the training fold only. It scores each weight by the AUROC of the rank-blend of the RF's out-of-bag predictions and the LR's out-of-fold predictions from the same grouped inner splits. That makes the ensemble a small, cheap stacking step.

The pooled oral-pathogen features were among the most useful changes (round 1), but they cover only five genera. CRC meta-analyses (Wirbel 2019, Thomas 2019) report a wider replicated oral and anaerobic-coccus consortium that also includes Solobacterium, Anaerococcus, Peptoniphilus, Campylobacter and Filifactor. Each of these is too rare in Baxter to be useful as a column on its own. This change adds a second pooled pair of features over the extended consortium: log of its combined abundance and how many of its genera are present. Both the random forest and the logistic regression can then use a dense, graded "oral invasion" score that matches across studies by taxonomy name. The original five-marker features are left unchanged.

The CRC signal in Baxter combines a few strong, sparse markers (oral pathogens, diversity, dysbiosis index) with a weak shift spread across many commensal genera. The current L2 logistic regression shrinks all ~100 standardized CLR genera evenly and can't drop noisy ones. Round 10 showed that hand-boosting the known markers hurts, so this change lets the training fold decide how sparse the model should be: the L2 model becomes an elastic-net whose L1 share (l1_ratio ∈ {0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8}) and C are chosen together by inner grouped CV. l1_ratio = 0 is pure L2, so the current model stays one of the options.

I'm adding a regularized CatBoost model (shallow depth-4 trees, small learning rate, ordered boosting, which suits about 230 samples) on the same features the forest uses. Unlike the forest it adds trees one after another, so it can pick up joint effects such as "oral pathogens present and commensals lost" and weaker additive genus effects the forest misses. It takes half of the tree side's blend weight (RF 0.25, CatBoost 0.25, LR 0.5), so the tuned forest and the CLR elastic net keep their current influence.

The forest currently chooses its split thresholds as the best cut-point among about 230 noisy, zero-inflated abundances. Those cut-points overfit, and they also don't transfer to studies with different depths. Extremely randomized trees draw their thresholds at random, which gives smoother, lower-variance scores for ranking. So the existing out-of-bag search on the training fold now also chooses between RF and ExtraTrees (bootstrapped, so OOB scoring still works), and the current RF stays one of the options.

Right now each CLR genus is standardized to unit variance before the elastic-net. For rare genera most of the variance comes from imputed zeros and depth noise, so standardizing gives them as much weight as abundant genera that actually shift (lost Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae commensals). This change adds a second option that scales the CLR block with one shared factor, so the penalty works in true log-ratio units and genera with high biological variance are favoured. Inner grouped CV on the training fold picks between the two scalings, and the current per-genus standardization stays one of the options.

ExtraTrees draws each split threshold uniformly between the feature's minimum and maximum in the node. On zero-inflated, right-skewed relative abundances, most of those draws land in the sparse upper tail and split off only a few outliers. Feeding the tree block log10(relative abundance + 1e-5) puts the random thresholds where the samples actually are. This transform is monotone and keeps ties, so the RF candidate is unaffected and the out-of-bag search can still pick it.

Right now inner CV on about 230 samples picks one CLR scaling (per-genus or shared) for the elastic-net. The two options score close to each other, so which one wins is mostly noise, and each fold may get a different model. The two scalings also pick up different signal: per-genus scaling weights rare genera equally, while shared scaling favours abundant commensals that shift a lot. This change keeps both elastic-nets, each still with its own C and L1 share tuned by inner grouped CV, and rank-averages them on the linear side, which should give a more stable and complementary linear score.
